opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difficulty is that the value of a pretrained embodied model doesn't show up where people instinctively look for it.

With language models, you can type a question and immediately see whether the answer is good. The capability is legible to anyone. With embodied intelligence, what people want to see is a robot doing something impressive, folding laundry, cooking, tidying a room. But a pretrained model's real contribution usually isn't that a single demo becomes possible. A well-engineered system with enough task-specific data and tuning can produce a nice demo without much pretraining at all. So when you show a demo, the natural reaction is, "Couldn't you have done that anyway?" Often the honest answer is yes, for that one task.

Where pretraining actually pays off is in things that are hard to film. How much less data you need to adapt to a new task. How gracefully the system handles a lighting change, a different object, an unexpected disturbance. Whether moving to a new embodiment takes weeks instead of months. Those are curves and ratios, not moments. They show up as efficiency and robustness across many tasks, and that kind of value is statistical. It's very hard to convey in a thirty-second video, and harder still to someone deciding whether to invest or adopt.

There's also a measurement problem. In language we have shared benchmarks and a common sense of what "better" means. In robotics, evaluation is expensive, physical, and hard to reproduce. Different labs use different hardware, environments, and success criteria. So even when a pretrained model really is better, it's difficult to prove it in a way others will trust and compare.

And the field is early. We're still debating what the right pretraining data is: internet video, simulation, teleoperation, human demonstrations. We're debating what the right representations and action spaces are. When the foundation itself is still moving, it's natural for people to be skeptical of claims about its value. So I see this as partly a communication challenge and partly a reflection of where we really are. Over time, I think the value becomes obvious not through one spectacular demo, but when people notice that building the next capability keeps getting cheaper and faster. That accumulation is the real story, and it's just slower to tell.

r001.rationale: The response discusses difficulty measuring and comparing results, but does not identify the difficulty of determining whether poor post-training results come from the training process, collected data, or the pretrained model.

r002.rationale: It mentions task-specific data, tuning, and engineering, but does not attribute the difficulty of demonstrating model quality to the expertise required to make the model usable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core difficulty is that a pretrained embodied model doesn't produce anything you can show someone directly. With a language model, you type a question, it answers, and in five seconds a non-technical person understands what changed. With an image or video model, you can play the clip and the quality speaks for itself. But a pretrained embodied model, by itself, is just a representation. It hasn't done anything in the physical world yet. Its value only becomes visible after you fine-tune it on a specific robot, for a specific task, in a specific environment, and then compare it against a model trained from scratch. That comparison is the entire story, and it's a story about a counterfactual, which is inherently hard to tell.

The second problem is that the visible part of the demo is almost always the hardware. When people watch a robot fold a towel or pour water, what they see is the arm and the gripper. They attribute the capability to the robot, not to the model behind it. And frankly, many impressive demos today are still heavily engineered for that one scene, so even people inside the field have trouble distinguishing "this is a generalizable foundation" from "this is a beautifully tuned single-task system." If experts struggle to tell them apart from a video, you can't expect investors or the public to.

Third, the benefits we care about, things like sample efficiency, robustness to lighting or object changes, transfer across embodiments, are all statistical properties. They show up as curves, not moments. A thirty percent reduction in demonstrations needed is a huge deal for anyone actually deploying robots, but it doesn't make a compelling thirty-second clip. There's no "wow" frame.

And finally, I think the field itself hasn't converged on what the pretrained thing should even be. Is it a visual encoder? A world model? A vision-language-action policy? Different groups mean different things when they say "embodied foundation model," so when you try to explain the value, you first have to spend ten minutes defining the object. Language models never had that problem; everyone agreed what a language model was. So part of the communication gap is really a maturity gap, and I expect it to close as the abstraction stabilizes and we have a few deployments where the model, not the hardware, is clearly the thing that made the difference.

r001.rationale: The response says value is shown by comparing fine-tuning against training from scratch, but does not identify difficulty separating poor results caused by training, data, or the pretrained model.

r002.rationale: It describes fine-tuning on a specific robot and task, but does not attribute the difficulty of demonstrating the model’s quality to the expertise required to make it usable.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that pretraining creates a capability that is hard to demonstrate directly. With a language model, you can ask a question and immediately see an answer. With embodied intelligence, what you see is a robot completing a task, and that result depends on the whole system—the hardware, the controller, the environment, and the model. So it’s difficult to isolate what the pretrained model contributed.

Its value may become clearer when you give the robot a new task. How much additional data does it need? How quickly can it adapt? Does it still work when the environment changes? A successful demonstration doesn’t necessarily answer those questions. You need comparisons across tasks and conditions to show that pretraining makes learning easier and more reliable. That’s a much harder story to communicate than a single impressive demo.

r001.rationale: The response says outcomes depend on the whole system, but does not identify poor post-training results or distinguish the training process, collected data, and pretrained model as possible causes.

r002.rationale: The response discusses hardware, controllers, and environments, but does not attribute the difficulty to the expertise required to make the model usable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that the value of pretraining is indirect. People can easily understand a robot completing a task: it picks something up, opens a door, or folds a piece of clothing. But when you show them a pretrained model, they naturally ask, “What can it do right now?” Its value may actually be that it makes learning the next task easier, requires less task-specific data, or adapts better to a new environment. Those benefits are harder to show in a short demo.

There’s also a measurement problem. If a robot succeeds, you’re seeing the whole system—the model, the hardware, the data, and the engineering. It’s difficult to isolate how much the pretrained model contributed. To communicate that value convincingly, we need comparisons: with and without pretraining, how much effort does it take to reach the same performance, and how well does that performance carry over to unfamiliar situations? That makes the benefit much more concrete.

r001.rationale: The response says it is difficult to isolate the pretrained model’s contribution from hardware, data, and engineering, but does not identify difficulty tracing poor post-training results to the training process, collected data, or pretrained model.

r002.rationale: The response discusses difficulty demonstrating a model’s value, but does not attribute that difficulty to the expertise required to make the model usable.
